cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for a deputy sheriff and a DSS social worker, holding that SDCL 26-8A-14 immunizes public officials involved in child abuse reporting and investigation and that mere negligence in the investigation does not defeat the statute's good-faith requirement.
cases.quote: Within the bounds of our statute, negligence and lack of good faith are not equivalent.

relevance.INP-01: This is South Dakota's leading construction of the SDCL 26-8A-14 immunity that protects mandatory reporters and the officials who act on their reports, and it fixes good faith - not due care - as the operative test.
relevance.INP-02: It extends the same good-faith immunity to any person who reports or cooperates in a child abuse investigation, which is the legal backdrop for non-mandated third-party reports.
relevance.INP-03: The immunized defendants included a county deputy sheriff who jointly interviewed the child with DSS, so the case governs the law-enforcement side of a referral.
relevance.INP-06: Because immunity turns on good faith rather than accuracy, an intake report that proves unfounded still carries no civil exposure for the reporter.
relevance.INP-07: The negligence alleged was the failure to request a medical examination of the child, placing the medical-evaluation step squarely inside the immunity.
relevance.INP-08: The statute's protection runs to the professional categories that make school-based reports, and this case sets the good-faith standard they are measured against.
relevance.DEC-02: Once a report is accepted, this case tells the investigator that a negligent investigation is immunized so long as the investigator held an honest belief in the suitability of the actions taken.
relevance.ACT-06: The claimed failure here was not obtaining prompt medical evaluation of a child suspected of being abused, the exact decision point at issue.
relevance.FAIL-04: It forecloses a negligence damages theory against county and DSS personnel whose investigative failures precede later serious harm to the child, absent bad faith.

cases.holding: The court reversed the denial of summary judgment and ordered judgment for two DSS social workers, holding they were immune under SDCL 26-8A-14 because the children produced only evidence of negligent investigation, not of bad faith.
cases.quote: These circumstances might amount to negligence but they do not equate with bad faith.

relevance.INP-01: It confirms that the SDCL 26-8A-14 good-faith shield covers the caseworkers who receive and act on referrals, not just the person who makes the report.
relevance.INP-05: The referrals here came from within the family's orbit, and the case sets what a family must later prove to hold the responding workers liable.
relevance.INP-06: Multiple hotline-type referrals were made and not acted on; the court held that inaction that is merely negligent remains immunized.
relevance.DEC-01: This is the controlling South Dakota authority on liability for screening out or under-investigating referrals - only bad faith, not error, is actionable.
relevance.DEC-02: It defines the legal consequence of accepting a referral and then investigating it poorly: immunity absent proof of improper motive.
relevance.DEC-06: Where the agency chooses in-home monitoring over removal, this case holds that choice is protected unless made in bad faith.
relevance.OUT-05: It shows that closing or not escalating a case, even wrongly, does not create civil liability without bad faith.
relevance.OUT-06: The children suffered years of sexual abuse after the workers declined to remove them, and the court still found immunity, defining the ceiling on fatality and serious-injury claims.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the South Dakota answer to a claim that the agency's failure to act caused grave harm to a child under its watch.

cases.holding: The court held that DSS employees owed a common law duty to protect a child from a foster child with known dangerous propensities and reversed summary judgment because fact issues remained on whether the employees acted in good faith under SDCL 26-8A-14.
cases.quote: it is clear the immunity provisions of SDCL 26-8A-14 apply to the placement activities of DSS employees involving JH

relevance.INP-01: The opinion sets out the full text and reach of SDCL 26-8A-14, the immunity provision that anchors South Dakota's mandatory reporting scheme.
relevance.INP-02: It confirms that the statute's immunity extends to any person who in good faith cooperates with DSS, which covers voluntary reporters.
relevance.INP-08: School and agency personnel participated in the foster care team meetings at issue, and the court treated withholding information from caregivers as evidence bearing on good faith.
relevance.ACT-03: It establishes an affirmative duty on DSS placement staff to share what they know about a foster child's dangerous propensities with the receiving foster home.
relevance.OUT-06: Where a child is seriously harmed in connection with a DSS placement, this case supplies the duty analysis and the bad-faith exception to statutory immunity.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the leading South Dakota decision permitting a damages claim to survive summary judgment when DSS placement conduct arguably lacked good faith.
relevance.PMC-04: The court's reliance on DSS's own procedures manual and administrative rules shows how internal standards become evidence in a post-harm review.

cases.holding: The court held that the circuit court erred by treating the mother's stipulation as an adjudication binding the father and by denying him an adjudicatory hearing, but affirmed the termination because on this record the error was harmless beyond a reasonable doubt.
cases.quote: the court could only dispense with an adjudicatory hearing if all of the necessary parties, including the father, agreed

relevance.INP-04: It holds that both parents are necessary parties who must be summoned and heard once a petition opens the case, whatever the referral source.
relevance.DEC-05: This is the controlling South Dakota statement that filing a petition triggers an adjudicatory hearing for every non-admitting parent under SDCL 26-7A-55.
relevance.ACT-05: Dispositional relief short of termination still depends on a valid adjudication reached with all necessary parties before the court.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the South Dakota template for attacking a defective adjudication on appeal - and the leading illustration of the harmless-error limit on that attack.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the adjudication and termination, holding that the State proved abuse and neglect by clear and convincing evidence and that DSS need not exhaust every possible form of assistance before termination becomes the least restrictive alternative.
cases.quote: The State has the burden of proving that the children were abused or neglected by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.INP-01: The case began when a school principal observed marks on a child and called DSS, the paradigm mandatory-reporter chain in South Dakota.
relevance.INP-03: Police officers accompanied the DSS worker, photographed injuries and interviewed the child, showing the joint law-enforcement/CPS response the court approved.
relevance.INP-08: The reporting educator's observation and the child's disclosure to her were treated as competent evidence supporting adjudication.
relevance.INP-12: Police placed the children in protective custody at a shelter before any court order, and the court reviewed that sequence without disturbing it.
relevance.DEC-05: It states the evidentiary burden the State carries once it files the petition and proceeds to the adjudicatory hearing.
relevance.ACT-01: The parents' participation in offered counseling and services is weighed here as part of the reasonable-efforts and least-restrictive-alternative analysis.
relevance.ACT-02: It holds that when court-ordered counseling and therapy fail to improve parenting, termination is justified and no narrower alternative remains.
relevance.ACT-05: Short-term protective placement at a domestic abuse shelter is treated as a lawful interim protective measure pending adjudication.
relevance.OUT-01: The reasonable-efforts findings here define when reunification ceases to be the required goal in South Dakota.
relevance.OUT-02: It supplies the standard of review for the ultimate finding that termination is the least restrictive alternative commensurate with the child's best interests.

cases.holding: The court raised the burden on a party opposing an ICWA transfer to clear and convincing evidence of good cause (prospectively), affirmed the denial of transfer because the moving tribe was not the Indian child's tribe, and affirmed termination on qualified expert testimony and proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
cases.quote: the standard most consistent with the Act requires clear and convincing evidence of good cause for a state court to refuse to transfer to tribal court

relevance.INP-11: This is South Dakota's governing decision on ICWA transfer: presumptive tribal jurisdiction, the burden on the opponent, and the requirement that a single tribe be designated the Indian child's tribe.
relevance.OUT-02: It applies 25 U.S.C. 1912(f)'s beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard and qualified expert witness requirement to termination of parental rights.
relevance.OUT-05: The first petition in this same family was dismissed after the court declined to find the children abused and neglected, illustrating dismissal at adjudication.

cases.holding: The court remanded a termination of parental rights because the circuit court never made the 25 U.S.C. 1912(f) finding, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the mother's continued custody would likely cause serious emotional or physical damage to the Indian child.
cases.quote: The court erred when it terminated Mother's parental rights without conducting this necessary examination utilizing the proper standard of proof.

relevance.INP-05: The case began when the mother herself contacted DSS about suspected abuse of her daughter, the self-report pathway, and the agency's response then turned on her.
relevance.INP-11: It enforces the ICWA-specific findings and qualified expert witness requirements that attach the moment an Indian child is involved.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the controlling South Dakota holding that the ICWA serious-damage finding is a separate, indispensable predicate to termination.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a recent example of the South Dakota Supreme Court vacating a dispositional order for failure to apply the correct standard of proof.

cases.case_name: People ex rel. South Dakota Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The court adopted abuse of discretion as the standard of review and held that deviation from ICWA's placement preferences must be supported by clear and convincing evidence of good cause, then affirmed the out-of-preference adoptive placement after a diligent but unsuccessful search.
cases.quote: we conclude that deviations from the ICWA placement preferences require a showing of good cause by clear and convincing evidence

relevance.INP-11: It sets the South Dakota evidentiary standard for departing from ICWA's statutory ordering of placements for an Indian child.
relevance.ACT-03: Any foster or pre-adoptive placement of an Indian child outside the ICWA preferences must be justified by clear and convincing evidence of good cause.
relevance.ACT-04: It requires a documented diligent search for extended family and tribal placements before a non-preferred placement can stand.
relevance.OUT-02: The adoptive placement decision reviewed here shows how the preference analysis controls the final permanency outcome.

cases.holding: The court held that ASFA's aggravated-circumstances exception to reasonable efforts does not override ICWA's active efforts requirement, but affirmed termination because DSS in fact continued to provide active efforts that proved unsuccessful.
cases.quote: Under ICWA, DSS was bound by law to make "active efforts" to reunite J.S.B with his father, but it was not required to persist with futile efforts.

relevance.INP-11: It is the leading South Dakota decision on how ICWA's active efforts mandate interacts with, and survives, federal ASFA shortcuts.
relevance.DEC-06: The mutual Family Service Agreement the court accepted as active efforts is the model for a services-first, non-punitive response.
relevance.ACT-01: The court treated a signed, voluntary Family Service Agreement offered in jail as satisfying the active efforts obligation.
relevance.OUT-01: It defines the point at which reunification efforts may lawfully stop - when they have proved unsuccessful, not merely inconvenient.
relevance.FAIL-03: It holds that a state agency cannot use one federal statute's exception to excuse noncompliance with another federal statute's mandate.
relevance.PMC-01: It shows a state court policing federal child-welfare compliance directly, rather than deferring to the agency's reading of federal law.

cases.holding: The court reversed the final dispositional order and remanded, holding the circuit court abused its discretion by denying the mother's and the tribe's ICWA transfer motions without an evidentiary hearing and without specific factual findings on good cause.
cases.quote: The circuit court was required to conduct an evidentiary hearing on the question whether good cause existed to deny Mother's and the Tribe's motions to transfer

relevance.INP-03: The case arose from a police response to an injury call at which officers saw drug paraphernalia and removed the children, the law-enforcement referral pathway.
relevance.INP-11: It is the controlling South Dakota holding that an ICWA transfer motion cannot be denied on argument alone - a hearing and written findings are required.
relevance.INP-12: Law enforcement, not DSS, effected the removal, and the opinion recites that sequence as the case's starting posture.
relevance.DEC-04: It illustrates the immediate removal decision made by officers at the scene and the judicial review that must follow.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a recent reversal of a dispositional order for procedural failure at the transfer stage, showing the appellate remedy for skipped hearings.

cases.holding: The court held the circuit court abused its discretion by granting a tribe's late oral transfer motion without hearing the available testimony of the child's physician, and reversed for a properly developed record on good cause.
cases.quote: circuit courts need the benefit of a sufficiently developed record to assist in the good cause determination

relevance.INP-11: It is the converse of A.O.: a transfer granted on a thin record is as reversible as a transfer denied on one, so the record requirement cuts both ways.

cases.holding: The court affirmed an abuse and neglect adjudication of an infant with non-accidental head trauma, holding the adjudication concerns the child's status so no parent-specific findings were required, and that a parent's remedy for an erroneous central registry listing lies with the Department, not the juvenile court.
cases.quote: Mother's remedy is with the Department rather than the juvenile court that is adjudicating the status of the child

relevance.INP-07: Treating physicians determined the injuries were non-accidental and reported them as potential child abuse, the medical-disclosure trigger.
relevance.INP-10: It explains how a hospital report escalates into protective custody and a filed petition, and what findings that escalation does and does not require.
relevance.DEC-03: It is the controlling South Dakota authority that an adjudication of the child's status is what places a name on the central registry, and that the registry challenge runs through DSS under ARSD 67:14:39.
relevance.DEC-05: It holds that a petition adjudicates the child's status, not the relative fault of each parent, which shapes what the State must plead and prove.
relevance.ACT-06: Emergency medical treatment of the critically injured infant, and the medical testimony about it, framed the entire adjudication.
relevance.OUT-01: After a period of State supervision the child was returned to the mother and the case was dismissed, the reunification endpoint.
relevance.OUT-05: The case was dismissed after supervision, illustrating closure without termination even where the adjudication was affirmed.
relevance.OUT-06: The child's near-fatal injuries and the medical proof of non-accidental trauma show the evidentiary shape of a serious-injury case.

cases.case_name: DuBray v. South Dakota Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The court affirmed reversal of a central registry listing, holding that DSS's exclusive reliance on an intake worksheet, a police incident report and a DSS narrative - all inadmissible hearsay - deprived DuBray of a meaningful due process hearing.
cases.quote: the admission of such evidence deprived DuBray of her fundamental right to a meaningful, due process hearing

relevance.INP-06: The DSS intake worksheet generated from the initial report was one of the hearsay documents held inadmissible to prove the allegation.
relevance.INP-10: It shows what happens when a screened-in report is substantiated on paper alone without producing the workers or officers who gathered the facts.
relevance.DEC-01: It marks the evidentiary line between an unreviewable internal screening judgment and a substantiation that must survive a contested hearing.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the leading South Dakota due process decision on substantiated findings and central registry placement - the subject may confront and cross-examine the witnesses against her.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the clearest South Dakota example of a court reversing an agency child-protection decision for procedural due process failure.

cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of a declaratory judgment action attacking a central registry listing, holding that the SDCL 26-8A-11 administrative decision had to be appealed under SDCL ch. 1-26 and that the failure to do so was a jurisdictional defect.
cases.quote: The Smalls' decision not to appeal pursuant to SDCL ch 1-26 deprived the circuit court of jurisdiction.

relevance.INP-10: It maps the statutory route from a substantiated investigation through informal review to a contested administrative hearing under SDCL 26-8A-11.
relevance.DEC-01: It explains that where there has been a court finding of abuse or neglect, the report's accuracy is conclusively presumed and no accuracy hearing is available.
relevance.DEC-03: It is the controlling South Dakota decision on the procedure and deadlines for challenging a central registry listing.
relevance.OUT-05: Even after the underlying case ended, the registry consequence persisted, showing that case closure does not clear the record.
relevance.FAIL-01: It defines the only procedural vehicle that can produce judicial reversal of a DSS registry decision - a timely SDCL ch. 1-26 appeal.
relevance.FAIL-06: The listing surfaced only through a tribal foster-care screening, illustrating how registry information is disclosed and how little recourse attaches after the appeal window closes.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the South Dakota authority on a citizen's ability to obtain judicial review of what the State holds about them in the child abuse registry.

cases.case_name: People ex rel. South Dakota Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The court held that the circuit court erred in letting an indigent mother proceed pro se at the adjudicatory hearing without the procedures that safeguard the SDCL 26-7A-31 right to counsel, but found the error harmless on the facts and affirmed termination.
cases.quote: SDCL 26-7A-31 specifically provides for a court appointed attorney for parents in an abuse and neglect proceeding.

relevance.DEC-05: It fixes the statutory right to appointed counsel that attaches to parents once a petition is filed and an adjudicatory hearing is set.
relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered conditions and services flowing from adjudication were imposed on a parent who had no lawyer, which is what the court held was error.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is South Dakota's statement that criminal-law waiver-of-counsel safeguards apply in abuse and neglect cases, and the leading counterexample of harmless-error affirmance.

cases.case_name: People ex rel. South Dakota Department of Social Services ex rel. A.D.
cases.holding: The court held that appointed counsel in a parental termination appeal may file a Korth (Anders-type) brief when no non-frivolous issue exists, because counsel's duties to an indigent client are the same in a civil termination appeal as in a criminal appeal.
cases.quote: counsel's submission of a Korth brief in this termination of parental rights case was procedurally appropriate and the State's arguments to the contrary are rejected

relevance.FAIL-01: It is the controlling South Dakota decision on appellate procedure and the effective-assistance obligations of appointed counsel in abuse and neglect appeals.

cases.case_name: People ex rel. South Dakota Department of Social Services ex rel. B.H.
cases.holding: The court denied reinstatement of a father's appeal from a termination order, holding that the SDCL 15-26A-4 requirement that the appellant personally sign the notice of appeal is jurisdictional and cannot be waived.
cases.quote: Because the signing requirement of SDCL 15-26A-4 is jurisdictional and jurisdictional requirements cannot be waived, the petition for reinstatement is denied.

relevance.FAIL-01: It is the South Dakota trap door on appellate review of terminations: a defective or untimely notice of appeal ends the case regardless of the merits.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of parental rights, holding that active efforts were provided, that termination was the least restrictive alternative, and that proceeding while the mother was mentally incompetent did not, on these facts and under the Mathews factors, violate due process.
cases.quote: Under the circumstances presented here, the circuit court did not violate Mother's due process rights in denying her request to continue the final dispositional hearing.

relevance.ACT-01: The opinion catalogues the voluntary services offered to the parents and treats their refusal as central to the active-efforts finding.
relevance.ACT-02: It reviews the court-ordered service plan and the interaction between SDCL 26-8A-26.1 good cause and the least restrictive alternative requirement.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding the circuit court did not clearly err in finding that further reasonable efforts would be futile and that statutory good cause under SDCL 26-8A-21.1 and 26-8A-26.1 justified terminating the parents' rights.
cases.quote: the court had sufficient evidence and reasoning to find Mother's efforts futile when considering the children's best interests

relevance.INP-05: DSS involvement began with a treatment-provider referral about the mother's prenatal substance use, a front-end help-seeking contact that escalated.
relevance.DEC-06: It shows how a front-end, services-based response can be exhausted and converted into a petition when the underlying risk persists.
relevance.ACT-02: It is the South Dakota authority on when a court-ordered service plan may be declared futile rather than extended.
relevance.OUT-01: It defines the futility limit on the reunification goal and places the burden on parents to show the futility finding was clearly erroneous.

cases.holding: The court affirmed DSS's consent to adoption by the foster parents over a maternal aunt, holding that the SDCL 26-7A-19.1 relative placement preference is conditioned on the placement being in the child's best interest and operates only as a tiebreaker.
cases.quote: if placement of the child with the relative serves the child's best interest to the same extent as placement with a nonrelative, DSS must place the child with the relative

relevance.ACT-04: This is South Dakota's controlling construction of the statutory kinship preference and its best-interest precondition.
relevance.OUT-03: It governs how a relative seeking kinship permanency must establish, not assume, that the preference applies to her.

cases.case_name: Matter of the Adoption of A.A.B. & B.A.B.
cases.holding: On intermediate appeal the court affirmed denial of DSS's motions to dismiss, holding that foster parents have standing under SDCL ch. 25-6 to petition to adopt children in DSS custody and that DSS consent is not a prerequisite to a circuit court adoption order.
cases.quote: DSS is not a party whose consent is necessary before a circuit court may order adoption of a child

relevance.OUT-02: It is the controlling South Dakota holding that the agency cannot gatekeep who may file an adoption petition for a child in its custody.

cases.case_name: In re Adoption of a Child Known as D.M.
cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of a great-aunt and great-uncle's motion to intervene in the adoption, holding that adoption is a creature of statute and that the adoption statutes give relatives no right to intervene, and that a DSS procedures manual creates no legally protectable interest.
cases.quote: The adoption statutes, however, do not specifically give family members the right to intervene.

relevance.ACT-04: It holds that DSS's internal order-of-preference manual favoring birth family does not create an enforceable relative right to placement.
relevance.OUT-03: It defines the narrow window in which relatives may contest an adoptive placement - inside the abuse and neglect case, not in the later adoption.

cases.case_name: In re Guardianship of S.M.N., T.D.N. and T.L.N.
cases.holding: The court held that a petitioner seeking guardianship over a fit natural parent's objection must prove extraordinary circumstances by clear and convincing evidence, and affirmed in part and reversed in part the grandmother's permanent guardianship and the mother's visitation award.
cases.quote: the petitioner in a guardianship proceeding must demonstrate extraordinary circumstances by clear and convincing evidence to overcome a natural parent's presumptive right to custody

relevance.ACT-04: When a relative caregiver seeks legal custody rather than agency placement, this case sets the burden she must carry against the parent.
relevance.OUT-03: This is the controlling South Dakota standard for guardianship as a permanency outcome and the constitutional protection a fit parent retains.
relevance.OUT-04: It confirms that guardianship jurisdiction and visitation orders continue to govern the child's legal status through minority, the framework a youth ages out of.

cases.holding: The court affirmed appointment of the child's maternal aunt and uncle as guardians of an Indian child over the incarcerated father's objection, holding they qualified as extended family under ICWA's first preference and that the best-interest inquiry includes preserving tribal and cultural heritage.
cases.quote: In determining the suitability of a proposed guardian under both ICWA and the Guardianship Act, the circuit court must ultimately consider the child's "best interests."

relevance.OUT-03: It is South Dakota's leading decision on guardianship of an Indian child, merging ICWA's placement preferences with the Guardianship Act's best-interest test.

cases.holding: The court reversed an order directing the county to pay court-appointed counsel in a protection order proceeding, holding SDCL 26-8A-18 authorizes county payment only in proceedings whose particular subject is a child's status or condition as abused or neglected.
cases.quote: the circuit court lacked statutory authority in this case to order Minnehaha to pay appointed counsel's costs

relevance.INP-02: The protection order petition repeated child abuse allegations that DSS had already investigated and found unsupported, the classic third-party report in a custody dispute.
relevance.INP-04: It shows a civil court confronting child abuse allegations and the statutory limits on converting that proceeding into an abuse and neglect case.
relevance.DEC-01: DSS investigated the same allegations and found no evidence of abuse, and law enforcement declined charges - the unfounded outcome in practice.
relevance.ACT-05: This is the South Dakota decision on protection orders in which child abuse is alleged and on who pays for appointed counsel in that proceeding.

cases.case_name: Brown Eyes v. South Dakota Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for DSS and its social workers on foster parents' tort claims arising from a failed adoption of two Indian children, holding the workers were protected by good-faith immunity absent any showing of improper motive or dishonesty.
cases.quote: There is no showing of improper motive or dishonesty and no showing of bad faith.

relevance.ACT-03: It defines the limited recourse foster parents have against DSS for placement and permanency decisions made about children in their home.
relevance.FAIL-05: Foster parents alleging that the agency treated them unfairly in an ICWA-affected adoption must show bad faith, not merely disparate outcome.

cases.holding: The court reversed, holding that requiring lifetime sex offender registration for a juvenile adjudicated in juvenile court, with no removal mechanism comparable to that available to adults, denies juveniles equal protection under the federal and South Dakota Constitutions.
cases.quote: under the Equal Protection Clauses of the United States Constitution and the South Dakota Constitution, Z.B. and similarly situated juveniles are denied equal protection

relevance.OUT-04: It addresses the lifelong collateral consequences that follow a youth out of the juvenile system into adulthood and holds one of them unconstitutional.
relevance.FAIL-05: It is South Dakota's leading equal protection holding striking down differential treatment of children within the juvenile justice and child welfare system.

cases.case_name: Mercer v. South Dakota Attorney General Office
cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of a public records request for a death investigation file, holding SDCL 1-27-1.5(5) and SDCL 23-5-11 expressly exempt law enforcement investigative reports and confidential criminal justice information, and that no right to redaction or partial release exists.
cases.quote: The records developed or received by the agencies charged with the duty to investigate Benda's death constitute confidential criminal justice information as defined by statute.

relevance.INP-09: It shows the statutory ceiling on what an outside investigator or journalist can obtain to trigger or support oversight of a state agency.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is the controlling South Dakota decision on when the State may lawfully withhold investigative records from the public, and it points the remedy to the Legislature.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit-style requests for investigative files run into the same SDCL 1-27-1.5(5) exemption this case enforces.
relevance.PMC-03: Any citizen review body seeking underlying investigative records in South Dakota must reckon with this exemption.
relevance.PMC-04: A death investigation is precisely the record category held exempt here, which is the central obstacle to independent child fatality review.
relevance.PMC-05: This is South Dakota's leading Public Records Act decision and the baseline for any transparency demand directed at the State.
relevance.PMC-06: It marks the legal boundary of what data can be assembled about state investigative conduct without legislative change.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the order unsealing search warrant affidavits after the investigation closed, holding no statute entitles the implicated individual to inspect the affidavits or participate in redaction before unsealing, and the circuit court did not abuse its discretion in denying that request.
cases.quote: There is nothing in SDCL 23A-35-4.1 or SDCL 15-15A-13 that mandates the circuit court to allow such an inspection.

relevance.FAIL-06: It establishes that sealing of investigative court records in South Dakota is time-limited and that public access presumptively resumes when the investigation ends.
relevance.PMC-03: It supplies the mechanism by which an outside body can obtain sealed investigative court records once the investigation terminates.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the current South Dakota authority on public and press access to sealed court records and the limits of a subject's veto over disclosure.
relevance.PMC-06: It confirms that court-file transparency, unlike agency records, is governed by an unmistakable legislative command to unseal.

cases.case_name: Puffy's, LLC v. Department of Health
cases.holding: The court affirmed a writ of mandamus compelling the Department of Health to issue a registration certificate, holding that the plain text of its own administrative rule obligated the agency to act and that the applicant had no other adequate remedy.
cases.quote: We conclude that the text of ARSD 44:90:03:16 obligated the Department to issue the registration certificate to Puffy's, and Puffy's had a clear legal right to receive it.

relevance.INP-09: It is the current South Dakota statement that a state agency is bound by the plain text of its own administrative rules, the premise of any compliance audit.
relevance.FAIL-01: It shows mandamus as the vehicle for judicial correction when an agency departs from its own rule and no administrative appeal is available.
relevance.PMC-01: Performance obligations written into rule are judicially enforceable in South Dakota, which matters when federal review findings are translated into state rules.
relevance.PMC-02: It gives an audit finding of rule noncompliance a concrete judicial remedy rather than a purely political one.

cases.holding: The court affirmed an adjudication of dependency and neglect and a dispositional order temporarily removing custody from the mother, emphasizing that the disposition was not a termination of parental rights but a temporary placement open to periodic review and return.
cases.quote: It is a temporary placement subject to periodic review by the court.

relevance.ACT-03: It is South Dakota's early and still-cited statement that a dispositional removal is a reviewable temporary placement, not a permanent severance.
relevance.ACT-05: It frames temporary protective disposition as the less drastic alternative available short of termination.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit affirmed qualified immunity for South Dakota social workers who removed an eleven-week-old infant with seventeen broken bones for about seven months, holding their actions rested on reasonable suspicion of abuse and were not disproportionate.
cases.quote: the officials' actions must have been based on a reasonable suspicion of abuse and must not have been disproportionate under the circumstances

relevance.INP-07: The case was triggered by radiographic findings at a cardiology visit, the medical-disclosure entry point into the system.
relevance.DEC-02: It states the two-part balancing test South Dakota caseworkers are measured against once an investigation begins.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the Eighth Circuit's application of the reasonable-suspicion and proportionality test to an emergency removal of an infant by South Dakota social workers.
relevance.ACT-06: Medical evidence of non-accidental fractures is treated as the kind of information that justifies immediate protective action.
relevance.FAIL-02: It marks the boundary of a wrongful removal claim in South Dakota: proportionate action on reasonable suspicion defeats the claim even after a months-long separation.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit affirmed denial of a motion to dismiss a section 1983 action, holding that holding a sixteen-month-old child seventeen days before a due process hearing was not prompt and that the State, not the parent, bears the burden of initiating prompt post-deprivation proceedings.
cases.quote: Under the facts of this case, seventeen days was not a prompt hearing.

relevance.INP-12: It is the circuit's statement that protective custody without a prior hearing obliges the State to initiate judicial review promptly on its own motion.
relevance.DEC-04: It supplies the timing rule against which an emergency removal followed by delayed court review must be measured in the Eighth Circuit.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the leading Eighth Circuit authority that a prolonged pre-hearing detention of a child, and backdated or delayed petitions, state a section 1983 claim.

cases.case_name: Heartland Academy Community Church v. Waddle
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit affirmed injunctive relief, upholding the conclusion that a juvenile officer violated the Fourth Amendment both by obtaining ex parte removal orders through stale information and material omissions and by removing thirty-five children with no court order, probable cause, or exigent circumstances.
cases.quote: upon de novo review, we see no error in the legal conclusions on the reasonableness of the seizures and the Fourth Amendment violation

relevance.INP-12: It holds that a mass protective seizure without a court order, probable cause, or exigency is an unreasonable seizure of each child.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the Eighth Circuit's core authority that an ex parte removal order obtained on misleading or omitted facts will not insulate the removal decision.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the leading circuit case establishing that both order-less removals and orders procured by misrepresentation are actionable Fourth Amendment violations.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit restated the Heartland rule and affirmed judgment for the defendants, holding that because the social worker acted pursuant to a valid ex parte order supported by a reasonable suspicion of a threat to the child's welfare, there was no Fourth or Fourteenth Amendment violation.
cases.quote: the protective seizure of children occur pursuant to a court order, or, in the absence of a court order, pursuant to probable cause or exigent circumstances

relevance.INP-12: It gives the Eighth Circuit's three-branch rule that every protective seizure of a child must satisfy - court order, probable cause, or exigency.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the cleanest circuit statement of the constitutional test the emergency removal decision must meet.
relevance.FAIL-02: It supplies the rule a plaintiff must negate, and the safe harbor an official obtains, when the removal rests on a facially valid ex parte order.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment forbids a State from terminating parental rights on a mere preponderance of the evidence and requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.DEC-05: It is the federal constitutional floor that shapes what the State must ultimately be prepared to prove once it files a petition aimed at severance.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the governing federal standard of proof for termination of parental rights and the source of South Dakota's clear and convincing requirement.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that due process does not require appointed counsel in every parental termination proceeding and left the appointment decision to the trial court case by case, subject to appellate review, finding no error in the refusal to appoint counsel there.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.DEC-05: It is the federal baseline for the right to counsel in dependency and termination proceedings, against which South Dakota's broader statutory right under SDCL 26-7A-31 should be read.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that an unwed father was entitled as a matter of due process to a hearing on his fitness before his children could be taken from him, and that presuming all unwed fathers unfit denied him equal protection.
cases.quote: Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him

relevance.DEC-04: It is the federal source of the rule that the State must ordinarily adjudicate parental fitness before, not after, it takes custody of a child.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the foundational due process authority for claims that a child was removed without any individualized hearing on the parent's fitness.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's reasonable efforts requirement creates no privately enforceable right, so beneficiaries cannot sue to enforce it under the Act itself or under 42 U.S.C. 1983.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.INP-09: It explains why federal child welfare compliance is enforced through federal administrative oversight rather than private litigation.
relevance.OUT-04: Title IV-E extended foster care obligations, like other IV-E plan requirements, are federal funding conditions rather than individually enforceable rights.
relevance.FAIL-03: This is the controlling federal authority that a state's failure to meet Title IV-E plan requirements is remedied through federal funding mechanisms, not private suit.
relevance.PMC-01: It is why CFSR findings and program improvement plans are the operative accountability tool rather than court enforcement by affected families.
relevance.PMC-02: Federal audit and reimbursement mechanisms are the enforcement channel this decision leaves open.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen Review Panels and similar CAPTA structures are advisory precisely because the underlying federal conditions are not privately enforceable.
relevance.PMC-06: Any accountability analysis built on federal plan requirements must account for the absence of a private right of action to enforce them.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the Due Process Clause imposed no constitutional duty on county social services officials to protect a child from his father's violence where the child remained in his father's custody rather than state custody.
cases.quote: the Due Process Clauses generally confer no affirmative right to governmental aid, even where such aid may be necessary to secure life, liberty, or property interests

relevance.OUT-06: It is the controlling federal authority limiting constitutional liability when a child known to the agency is killed or gravely injured by a private actor.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the first obstacle in any section 1983 claim arising from a child's death under agency supervision, and it directs attention to whether the child was in state custody.
relevance.PMC-04: It is the reason child fatality accountability in the United States proceeds through review commissions and state tort law rather than federal constitutional suits.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court rejected every challenge to the Indian Child Welfare Act, upholding it against Article I and anticommandeering attacks on the merits and disposing of the equal protection and nondelegation claims for lack of standing.
cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

relevance.INP-11: It confirms that ICWA's placement preferences and procedural mandates bind South Dakota state courts and agencies in full force.
relevance.FAIL-03: It settles that a state cannot decline to apply ICWA on federalism grounds, so noncompliance is a compliance failure rather than a contested constitutional question.
relevance.FAIL-05: It leaves the equal protection challenge to ICWA's preferences unresolved on standing grounds, so race-based attacks on tribal placement preferences remain foreclosed in practice.
relevance.PMC-06: It fixes the current legal status of ICWA, the single largest federal overlay on state child welfare decision chains in South Dakota.

cases.case_name: People in the Interests of M.C.
cases.holding: The court reversed an order transferring an Indian child's abuse and neglect proceeding to tribal court, holding that although the tribe's motion was timely, the party opposing transfer was entitled to an evidentiary hearing and that the circuit court had to make specific findings on the good-cause factors.
cases.quote: M.C. was entitled to an evidentiary hearing to establish good cause not to transfer jurisdiction to the Tribe.

relevance.INP-11: It is South Dakota's foundational ICWA transfer decision - presumptively tribal jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. 1911(b), the burden on the party opposing transfer, and a mandatory evidentiary hearing with specific findings on each good-cause factor - and it is the parent authority expressly relied on in People ex rel. T.I. and In re E.T.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the earliest South Dakota reversal of a transfer order entered on a perfunctory hearing with conclusory findings, and the template for the later reversals in Interest of A.O. and In re E.T.

cases.holding: The court affirmed a finding of good cause to deny the tribe's ICWA transfer motions, holding that the tribe had actual notice, that the State substantially complied with ICWA's notice requirement, and that the motions filed eleven and seventeen months after notice came at an advanced stage of the proceedings.
cases.quote: The Tribe had actual notice of the pending dispositional hearing, and by faxing notice of the hearing to the Tribe, the State substantially complied with ICWA.

relevance.INP-11: It is the South Dakota ICWA transfer decision immediately preceding People ex rel. T.I. and the controlling application of the advanced-stage/untimeliness good-cause factor, while also holding that the State's ICWA notice obligation continues after a tribe intervenes and is not satisfied merely when convenient.

cases.case_name: Matter of Dependency and Neglect of A.L.
cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of a tribe's petition to transfer a dependency and neglect proceeding, holding that the BIA good-cause guidelines are interpretive rather than binding and that the trial court was not clearly erroneous in finding the tribe's transfer request, made a year after notice, untimely.
cases.quote: We agree with State that the BIA guidelines are not binding. They are interpretative rather than legislative in nature.

relevance.INP-11: It is South Dakota's earliest construction of ICWA's undefined 'good cause to the contrary' and the source of the rule, relied on in 2011 S.D. 8 and In the Interest of D.M., that the BIA guidelines inform but do not bind the court and that timeliness is judged case by case.
relevance.ACT-04: Because the enumerated BIA factors are neither exhaustive nor binding, a South Dakota court weighing extended-family and tribal placement options is not confined to them when it assesses good cause.

cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for town and county officials sued after a four-year-old was mauled, holding that government owes its duty of protection to the public rather than to particular persons and that the special-duty exception requires actual knowledge coupled with at least one other Cracraft factor, none of which the plaintiffs established.
cases.quote: Only when actual knowledge is coupled with one or more of the other factors, can we uphold both the spirit and substance of the private duty exception.

relevance.FAIL-04: It is South Dakota's controlling statement of the public duty doctrine and the four-factor special-duty exception, the framework a family must satisfy before any state or county child-protection defendant owes a private tort duty for failing to protect a child.
relevance.OUT-06: Where a child is gravely injured after officials knew of a danger, this case fixes the limit on recovery: actual knowledge of the danger, standing alone, never creates a private duty.
relevance.ACT-03: E.P. v. Riley's duty analysis for DSS placement staff is an application of this framework, so Tipton supplies the governing test for any claim that the agency owed a private duty in placing or supervising a child.

cases.holding: The court affirmed an adjudication of abuse and neglect and termination of the father's parental rights, holding that the State proved abuse and neglect by clear and convincing evidence on the parents' history with their other children and that termination was the least restrictive alternative.
cases.quote: Termination of parental rights is proper only when the court finds by clear and convincing evidence that termination is the least restrictive alternative in keeping with the child's best interest.

relevance.DEC-05: It is the customary South Dakota primary citation for the clear-and-convincing burden and the standard of review that attach once the State files its abuse and neglect petition, and it is the authority In re S.A. cites on that point.
relevance.OUT-02: It states the SDCL 26-8A-27 rule that termination requires clear and convincing proof that severance is the least restrictive alternative in the child's best interest, and it holds ICWA's heightened standard inapplicable absent proof the child meets the Act's criteria.
relevance.INP-07: Hospital personnel reported the newborn's skull fractures and brain hemorrhage to DSS, the medical-disclosure entry point that opened the case.
relevance.INP-12: A police officer was called to the hospital and the infant was taken into protective custody there, before any petition was filed, on the strength of the parents' prior abuse and neglect history.

cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of a protection order and of a request to restrict visitation, holding the circuit court was not clearly erroneous in finding that the mother had failed to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the father sexually abused their child.
cases.quote: Under SDCL 25-10-5, a circuit court may grant a protection order if it finds by a preponderance of the evidence that abuse has occurred.

relevance.INP-04: The circuit court itself drove the fact-finding, ordering psychological and psychosexual evaluations and receiving the results of five separate agency investigations, the court-directed referral pathway in a visitation dispute.
relevance.ACT-05: It is South Dakota's statement of the SDCL 25-10-5 preponderance standard governing a protection order sought on child abuse allegations, and of the clearly-erroneous review that follows.
relevance.DEC-01: Three South Dakota CPS investigations and two Nebraska investigations were all closed as 'unsubstantiated' or 'unfounded,' showing the screen-out and unfounded outcome as it actually reaches a court.
relevance.INP-02: Repeated parental and third-party reports routed through law enforcement, CPS in two states, a children's advocacy center and treating clinicians illustrate how a custody dispute generates voluntary reports and how they are weighed.

cases.holding: The court reversed and held that a city's confidential construction settlement agreement is a public record open to inspection, because the Public Records Act's presumption of openness and the SDCL 1-27-1.3 directive to construe fiscal records liberally require narrow construction of the SDCL 1-27-1.5(20) exception.
cases.quote: Therefore, in accordance with that presumption of openness and the requirement that we construe the statute liberally in favor of openness, we must narrowly construe the exception with subdivision (20).

relevance.PMC-05: It is the leading post-Mercer South Dakota Public Records Act decision and it construes the Act's exceptions narrowly against the government rather than deferring to the agency's characterization.
relevance.FAIL-06: It holds that a public body cannot defeat disclosure by having contracted for confidentiality, which is the answer to an agency that withholds records it agreed to keep secret.
relevance.PMC-02: SDCL 1-27-1.3 requires fiscal records, audits, vouchers and expenditure records to be construed liberally in favor of access, which is the statutory hook for any financial audit of South Dakota child-welfare spending.
relevance.PMC-06: Read with Mercer, it marks the two poles of South Dakota records law - investigative files are exempt, but fiscal and contractual records are presumptively open.

cases.holding: The court granted a permanent writ of prohibition against a circuit judge's closure and gag orders, holding that the First Amendment affords the media and public a qualified right of access to civil trials and adopting the Publicker requirement of an articulated overriding interest, specific findings, and narrow tailoring before closure.
cases.quote: We, therefore, hold that the First Amendment affords the media and public a qualified right of access to civil trials in this state.

relevance.PMC-05: It establishes the constitutional right of access to South Dakota civil trials and court records and the procedure a court must follow before closing either.
relevance.FAIL-06: A closure or sealing order entered without an articulated overriding interest, findings specific enough for appellate review, and narrow tailoring is subject to a writ of prohibition.
relevance.PMC-06: It is the access framework on which Matter of Implicated Individual builds, and the constitutional counterweight to the statutory exemptions enforced in Mercer.

cases.holding: The court held that a newspaper has standing to challenge an order sealing a criminal court file, declined to give a corrective nunc pro tunc order retroactive effect against the newspaper's pending access request, and granted mandamus directing access to the file as it existed up to the amended order.
cases.quote: Therefore, the Journal has standing to challenge the validity of Judge Callahan's October 4, 2021 seal order.

relevance.PMC-05: It is the most recent South Dakota decision on press access to court files, confirming that a newspaper denied access has standing and an adequate writ remedy.
relevance.FAIL-06: It holds that a court may not retroactively cure a premature seal through a nunc pro tunc order so as to extinguish a third party's already-pending access request.
relevance.PMC-06: Any current transparency analysis must account for it as the latest word on the timing and mechanics of access to sealed South Dakota court files.

notes: South Dakota has no intermediate appellate court. Every state-law case in this brief is a published opinion of the South Dakota Supreme Court (court_id 'sd'), retrieved from CourtListener in this session; no unpublished or memorandum decisions were used. Federal authority is drawn from the Eighth Circuit (South Dakota's circuit) and the U.S. Supreme Court.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the SD node files are keyword-matched noise. Of the twelve candidate titles present across the SD files (probate, trust, guardianship-of-adult and legislative-ethics matters, plus 'In re S.A.', 'Interest of J.W.', 'Interest of N.K.', 'In the Matter of the Adoption of I.V.E.'), only 'In re S.A.' was retrieved, read and found on point; it is included here as In re S.A., 2005 S.D. 120, 708 N.W.2d 673. All other candidate titles were discarded.

Statutory spine confirmed from the SD node files and from the opinions themselves: SDCL ch. 26-8A (reporting, immunity under 26-8A-14, central registry and its administrative review under 26-8A-11, reasonable efforts under 26-8A-21 and 26-8A-21.1, termination grounds under 26-8A-26 and 26-8A-26.1) and SDCL ch. 26-7A (temporary custody, parties and summons under 26-7A-43 to 26-7A-55, appointed counsel under 26-7A-31, relative placement preference under 26-7A-19.1, clear and convincing burden under 26-7A-82). Central registry listing criteria are in ARSD 67:14:39.

OUT-04 (extended foster care / aging out) has no on-point South Dakota Supreme Court authority. Repeated targeted searches for extended foster care, jurisdiction past age 18, and Chafee/FCSIAA transition services in court=sd returned nothing responsive. The node is therefore mapped to the federal standard - Suter v. Artist M. (Title IV-E plan requirements are funding conditions, not privately enforceable rights) - plus In re Guardianship of S.M.N. and People in Interest of Z.B. for the adjacent questions of continuing legal status and lifelong collateral consequences. A South Dakota youth denied extended care has, on current authority, no private federal cause of action and no reported state precedent.

DEC-06 (differential response / alternative response) likewise has no South Dakota decision using that vocabulary. The mapped cases (People ex rel. J.S.B., Jr.; Interest of M.S. & K.S.; Cotton v. Stange) are the closest functional authority: they govern voluntary service agreements accepted in lieu of compulsion, the point at which a services-first response may be declared futile, and the immunity of workers who choose in-home services over removal.

PMC-01 through PMC-06 are oversight and transparency nodes with no direct South Dakota child-welfare case law. They are mapped to the governing federal rule on enforceability of federal child-welfare plan requirements (Suter v. Artist M.), South Dakota's controlling public-records and court-record-access decisions (Mercer; Matter of Implicated Individual; and, added in this pass, Argus Leader Media v. Hogstad, Rapid City Journal v. Delaney and Rapid City Journal v. Callahan), and Puffy's, LLC v. Department of Health for the proposition that a South Dakota agency is bound by, and can be compelled by mandamus to follow, the plain text of its own administrative rules. Lawyers should treat these mappings as the nearest available authority, not as child-welfare-specific holdings.

FAIL-05 (discrimination / retaliation): no South Dakota decision addresses race or disability discrimination in child welfare placements. People in Interest of Z.B. is the state's leading equal protection holding affecting children in the juvenile system; Haaland v. Brackeen disposed of the equal protection challenge to ICWA's placement preferences on standing grounds, so that challenge remains unresolved on the merits. Brown Eyes supplies the good-faith-immunity obstacle facing foster parents who allege unfair agency treatment.

People in Interest of D.K. (1976) applied a preponderance standard at adjudication. That standard is superseded: SDCL 26-7A-82, People ex rel. D.T. (2003) and In re S.A. (2005) now require clear and convincing evidence. D.K. is cited here only for its enduring point that a dispositional removal is a temporary placement subject to periodic judicial review, not a severance.

In re C.V. and People ex rel. South Dakota Department of Social Services, 2004 S.D. 131 (C.R.) both found procedural error (denial of an adjudicatory hearing to a non-stipulating parent; letting an indigent parent proceed pro se without valid waiver) and then affirmed on harmless error. Counsel relying on either case for reversal must confront that limitation; the dissent in In re C.V. argued at length that Santosky forecloses harmless-error analysis, but that is a dissent and is not quoted here.

People ex rel. T.I. raised the burden for denying an ICWA transfer to clear and convincing evidence prospectively only. Cases decided before December 21, 2005 - including People in the Interests of M.C. (1993), Matter of Dependency and Neglect of A.L. (1989) and In the Interest of D.M. (2004) - were reviewed under abuse of discretion and the clearly-erroneous standard. Interest of A.O. (2017) and In re E.T. (2019) subsequently added the requirement of an evidentiary hearing and specific factual findings on good cause, in both directions.

In re E.T., 927 N.W.2d 111 (S.D. 2019), appears in CourtListener with no parallel S.D. public-domain citation in its cluster, so it is given here in N.W.2d form with the court designator. Interest of L.N., 2022 S.D. 8, and Puffy's, LLC v. Department of Health, 2025 S.D. 10, likewise have no N.W.2d citation in their CourtListener clusters and are cited in public-domain form only.

CourtListener records the Lassiter cluster's date_filed as 1981-08-28; the opinion itself issued June 1, 1981, and the August date corresponds to the denial of rehearing. The cluster value is reported in date_decided for traceability to the source.

Two closely related Eighth Circuit lines are both included for FAIL-02 and DEC-04 because they cut in opposite directions: Heartland (removal without order, probable cause or exigency, and orders obtained by misrepresentation, violate the Fourth Amendment) and Manzano/Abdouch (South Dakota DSS workers acting on reasonable suspicion, proportionately, receive qualified immunity). Riehm supplies the circuit's compact three-branch statement of the seizure rule. No published Eighth Circuit decision was found applying the Fourth Amendment to a caseworker's warrantless entry into a South Dakota home; searches on that point returned nothing responsive, and the node mappings reflect that gap.

No South Dakota Supreme Court decision was found on criminal liability for failure to report, on sibling-placement preference as a distinct doctrine, or on children missing from foster care. Searches for each returned nothing on point. INP-01 and INP-02 are therefore built on the civil immunity line (B.W. v. Meade County, Cotton v. Stange, E.P. v. Riley), which is where South Dakota's reporting law has actually been litigated.

Missing (for a later pass): People in Interest of M.C., 504 N.W.2d 598 (S.D. 1993) — the foundational South Dakota decision on good cause to deny an ICWA transfer and on the record a circuit court must develop; it is expressly relied on by both People ex rel. T.I. (¶19) and In re E.T. (¶16), which are in the brief, yet the parent case is absent from INP-11. [RESOLVED in this pass - see the 'Added' note below.]

Missing (for a later pass): In the Interest of D.M., 2004 S.D. 90, 685 N.W.2d 768 — South Dakota's ICWA transfer decision immediately preceding T.I., cited in T.I. for the proposition that mere discretion to override a transfer is inconsistent with congressional intent; a practitioner briefing INP-11 would expect it. [RESOLVED in this pass - see the 'Added' note below.]

Missing (for a later pass): Tipton v. Town of Tabor, 1997 S.D. 96, 567 N.W.2d 351 — South Dakota's controlling statement of the public duty doctrine and the special-duty exception. E.P. v. Riley is an application of Tipton; without it the duty analysis underpinning FAIL-04, OUT-06 and ACT-03 is presented without its governing framework. [RESOLVED in this pass - see the 'Added' note below.]

Missing (for a later pass): People ex rel. D.T., 2003 S.D. 88, 667 N.W.2d 694 — the case In re S.A. cites for the clear-and-convincing burden at adjudication and for the standard of review on abuse and neglect findings; it is the customary primary cite for DEC-05 and OUT-02 in South Dakota practice. [RESOLVED in this pass - see the 'Added' note below.]

Missing (for a later pass): In re A.L., 442 N.W.2d 233 (S.D. 1989) — South Dakota's early holding that the BIA good-cause factors are neither exhaustive nor binding, relied on in 2011 S.D. 8 (¶18); relevant to ACT-04 and INP-11. [RESOLVED in this pass - see the 'Added' note below.]

Missing (for a later pass): Argus Leader Media v. Hogstad, 2017 S.D. 57, 902 N.W.2d 778 — post-Mercer construction of the South Dakota Public Records Act; PMC-05 and FAIL-06 are built on a 2015 decision without the later authority. [RESOLVED in this pass - see the 'Added' note below.]

Missing (for a later pass): Rapid City Journal v. Delaney, 2011 S.D. 55, 804 N.W.2d 388 — South Dakota's decision on public and press access to court proceedings and records, which is the access framework Matter of Implicated Individual builds on; missing from PMC-05. [RESOLVED in this pass - see the 'Added' note below.]

Missing (for a later pass): Rapid City Journal v. Callahan, 2022 S.D. 38, 977 N.W.2d 742 — the most recent South Dakota public-records decision; any current transparency demand analysis under PMC-05, PMC-06 or FAIL-06 should account for it. [RESOLVED in this pass - see the 'Added' note below.]

Added People in the Interests of M.C., 504 N.W.2d 598 (S.D. 1993) (cluster 2220835), for INP-11 and FAIL-01: it is the foundational South Dakota ICWA transfer decision, holding that the party opposing transfer is entitled to an evidentiary hearing and that the circuit court must make specific findings on the good-cause factors rather than a conclusory 'no good cause to the contrary.' It is the parent authority expressly relied on by People ex rel. T.I. and In re E.T., both already in the brief.

Added In the Interest of D.M., 2004 S.D. 90, 685 N.W.2d 768 (cluster 901210), for INP-11: it is the ICWA transfer decision immediately preceding T.I. and the controlling South Dakota application of the advanced-stage/untimeliness good-cause factor (motions filed eleven and seventeen months after notice), while also holding that faxed notice plus actual notice constitutes substantial compliance and that the State's duty to keep an intervening tribe informed continues after initial notice. The verifier's characterization of D.M. as the source of the 'mere discretion to override a transfer is inconsistent with congressional intent' proposition was not located in the D.M. opinion text; that phrasing appears in T.I.'s discussion, and the holding stated here is taken from D.M.'s own majority opinion.

Added Tipton v. Town of Tabor, 1997 S.D. 96, 567 N.W.2d 351 (cluster 1714863), for FAIL-04, OUT-06 and ACT-03: it supplies the public duty doctrine and the four-factor Cracraft special-duty exception that E.P. v. Riley applies to DSS placement staff. Without it, the duty analysis underlying the South Dakota failure-to-protect and serious-injury nodes was presented without its governing framework; Tipton also establishes that actual knowledge of a danger, standing alone, never creates a private duty.

Added People ex rel. D.T., Jr., 2003 S.D. 88, 667 N.W.2d 694 (cluster 901073), for DEC-05, OUT-02, INP-07 and INP-12: it is the customary South Dakota primary citation for the clear-and-convincing burden at adjudication and for the SDCL 26-8A-27 least-restrictive-alternative standard at termination, and the case In re S.A. cites on those points. Its facts also supply a clean medical-disclosure-to-protective-custody sequence (hospital report of an infant's skull fractures, officer called to the hospital, custody taken before any petition).

Added Matter of Dependency and Neglect of A.L., 442 N.W.2d 233 (S.D. 1989) (cluster 1237582), for INP-11 and ACT-04: it is South Dakota's earliest construction of ICWA's undefined 'good cause to the contrary' and the source of the rule - relied on in 2011 S.D. 8 and In the Interest of D.M. - that the BIA guidelines are interpretive rather than binding and that timeliness is assessed case by case with flexibility.

Added Argus Leader Media v. Hogstad, 2017 S.D. 57, 902 N.W.2d 778 (cluster 4427727), for PMC-05, PMC-02, PMC-06 and FAIL-06: it is the leading post-Mercer South Dakota Public Records Act decision, holding that the Act's exceptions must be construed narrowly against the government and that a public body cannot defeat disclosure by contracting for confidentiality. Its reliance on SDCL 1-27-1.3's liberal-construction directive for fiscal and expenditure records is the statutory hook for any financial audit of South Dakota child-welfare spending, and it materially qualifies the impression left by Mercer alone.

Added Rapid City Journal v. Delaney, 2011 S.D. 55, 804 N.W.2d 388 (cluster 902061), for PMC-05, PMC-06 and FAIL-06: it holds that the First Amendment affords the media and public a qualified right of access to civil trials in South Dakota and adopts the Publicker procedure - articulated overriding interest, findings specific enough for appellate review, and narrow tailoring - that a court must follow before closing a proceeding or sealing records. It is the access framework on which Matter of Implicated Individual builds.

Added Rapid City Journal v. Callahan, 2022 S.D. 38, 977 N.W.2d 742 (cluster 9508040), for PMC-05, PMC-06 and FAIL-06: it is the most recent South Dakota decision on press access to court files, holding that a newspaper denied access has standing to challenge a sealing order and that a court may not give a corrective nunc pro tunc order retroactive effect so as to extinguish a third party's already-pending access request.

Added L.S. v. C.T., 2009 S.D. 2, 760 N.W.2d 145 (cluster 8279753), for INP-04, ACT-05, DEC-01 and INP-02: INP-04 previously rested on a single case (Pfuhl) in node_map, and this decision supplies a second, fuller illustration of a civil court directing its own fact-finding - court-ordered psychological and psychosexual evaluations, and the results of five separate CPS and law-enforcement investigations - on child abuse allegations raised in a visitation dispute. It also states the SDCL 25-10-5 preponderance standard for a protection order and shows the unfounded/unsubstantiated outcome as it reaches a court.

All eight authorities named by the verifier were located on CourtListener, their clusters and opinions retrieved, and their majority opinion text read in this session. None had to be discarded, and there is no named authority that could not be verified. Every quote in the nine new entries was checked programmatically to be an exact substring (whitespace and quotation marks normalized) of the retrieved majority opinion text, of thirty words or fewer, with no ellipses.

node_map correction: the prior node_map under-represented the brief, because several cases carried a relevance sentence for a node without being listed under it. Seven nodes (INP-02, INP-04, INP-05, INP-08, DEC-01, ACT-05, OUT-04) appeared to have only one case when in fact two or more already-verified cases addressed them. node_map has been rebuilt from the relevance objects plus this pass's additions, so no node now has fewer than two cases and none has more than six.

Because the two-to-six-case-per-node ceiling is binding, a few cases that carry a relevance sentence for a node are not listed under that node in node_map, where stronger authority already fills the six slots. This affects INP-11 (People ex rel. A.B., People ex rel. J.S.B., Jr., 2011 S.D. 8 and Haaland v. Brackeen retain their INP-11 relevance sentences but yield the map slots to the six controlling transfer/jurisdiction decisions), DEC-05 (In re M.V.), OUT-02 (2011 S.D. 8), FAIL-01 (Interest of C.V., People ex rel. A.B., 2004 S.D. 131, Puffy's) and PMC-06 (Rapid City Journal v. Callahan). Practitioners should read the relevance objects, not node_map alone, for the full set of authority bearing on a node.

Missing (for a later pass): State ex rel. J.J., 454 N.W.2d 317 (S.D. 1990) — the South Dakota ICWA good-cause decision expressly relied on in People in Interests of M.C. (the case remanded for an evidentiary hearing and then reviewed 'detailed findings of fact and conclusions of law' supporting good cause to deny transfer). It is the companion to M.C. on what a sufficient good-cause record looks like, and INP-11 is incomplete without it.

Missing (for a later pass): Matter of N.A.H., 418 N.W.2d 310 (S.D. 1988) — South Dakota's holding that ICWA notice must at a minimum conform to 25 U.S.C. 1912(a) and that the better practice is to follow the BIA guidelines. It is the predicate for In the Interest of D.M.'s substantial-compliance-by-fax holding, and INP-11 currently presents the notice rule only in its most permissive form.

Missing (for a later pass): Matter of S.D., 402 N.W.2d 346 (S.D. 1987) — the earliest South Dakota statement that the BIA guidelines 'do not have binding legislative effect,' relied on by the State and adopted in Matter of Dependency and Neglect of A.L. It is the true origin of the rule the brief attributes to A.L.

Missing (for a later pass): Tipton v. Town of Tabor, 538 N.W.2d 783 (S.D. 1995) (Tipton I) — the first appeal, which adopted the Cracraft four-factor special-duty test and held that 'any combination' of factors may suffice. Tipton II (in the brief) narrows that language; citing the 1997 decision alone presents the public duty doctrine without the case that created it, which matters for FAIL-04 and OUT-06.

Missing (for a later pass): Matter of J.A.H., 502 N.W.2d 120 (S.D. 1993) — the authority People ex rel. D.T. cites for the proposition that the State must prove abuse and neglect by clear and convincing evidence. It is the root citation in the DEC-05 chain and is absent.

Missing (for a later pass): In re A.S., 2000 S.D. 94, 614 N.W.2d 383 — holds it is incumbent on the party asserting ICWA's applicability to prove the child meets the Act's criteria. This is the rule that decided the ICWA issue in People ex rel. D.T. and it is the threshold question in every INP-11 case; it should be cited directly rather than through D.T.

Missing (for a later pass): Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield, 490 U.S. 30 (1989) — the Supreme Court's foundational ICWA decision on domicile and exclusive tribal jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. 1911(a). INP-11 currently maps only transfer cases under 1911(b) and federal authority only through Brackeen; the exclusive-jurisdiction branch is unrepresented.

Missing (for a later pass): Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) — the constitutional source of the fit-parent presumption that In re Guardianship of S.M.N. applies in requiring extraordinary circumstances by clear and convincing evidence. OUT-03 rests on that presumption without citing its federal basis.
